title: Github Fundamentals
description: Covers Giithub and Fundamentals around Github

questions.prompt: What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

options.text: Git is a program that runs on your computer; GitHub is a website that stores Git projects online
Git is for individuals; GitHub is the same program but for teams
Git is the paid version; GitHub is the free version
They are two names for the same thing

questions.prompt: A repository is best described as:

options.text: A backup copy of your hard drive
The list of people who have permission to edit a project
A single file with its edit history attached
One project — all its files, plus the complete history of every change ever made to them
A saved snapshot of your project at a moment in time, with a note explaining what changed and why
The act of publishing your project so the public can see it
Permission granted to another person to edit your project
A promise to finish a task by a deadline

questions.prompt: Which of these is TRUE about GitHub?

options.text: Anyone can edit your public repository directly without your approval
You choose whether each repository is public or private, and private repos are free
Everything you upload is automatically visible to the public
You must use the command line to create a repository

questions.prompt: Why would you create a branch?

options.text: To give a new team member their own private copy of the files
To work on changes without affecting the official version until you decide to
To permanently split a project into two separate projects
To create a backup in case your computer fails
A demand that a teammate finish their work before you can continue
A formal proposal to add your branch's changes to the official version, open for review and discussion
An automatic notification sent whenever a file changes
A request to download a copy of someone's project

questions.prompt: Why does the README file matter so much?

options.text: GitHub will not let you create a repository without one
It controls who has permission to access the project
It displays automatically beneath the files and is the first — often only — thing anyone reads
It is the file that stores your commit history

questions.prompt: Put the everyday loop in the correct order.

options.text: Branch → change → commit → pull request → merge
Commit → branch → change → merge → pull request
Change → commit → branch → merge → pull request
Pull request → branch → change → commit → merge

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a fork and a clone?

options.text: A fork is for public projects; a clone is for private ones
A fork is temporary; a clone is permanent
They are the same operation with different names
A fork is your own copy of someone's project on GitHub; a clone is a copy downloaded to your computer

questions.prompt: You accidentally commit a password to a repository, then delete it in your next commit. What should you do?

options.text: Nothing, as long as the repository is private
Nothing, deleting it in the next commit removes it completely
Assume the password is compromised and change it immediately
Rename the file so scanners cannot find it
